title: Two Degrees Weather
shortDescription: Every temperature in °F and °C at once, side by side. No converting, ever.
fullDescription:
Two Degrees shows the weather in Fahrenheit and Celsius at the same time, so you never have to convert again. Pick which unit is large; the other is always right beside it.

YOUR CITIES
• Swipe between up to 20 cities, each on its own sky
• Use My Location to see the weather where you are (optional; you can say no)
• Search any place in the world, even offline, from a built-in list of 34,000 places
• Reorder your list, and tap the temperature to swap which unit is large

THE FORECAST
• Right now: the temperature in °F and °C, the sky, and today's high and low in both units
• The next 24 hours, with rain chances and one plain sentence ("Warming to 53°F / 12°C by 2 PM")
• Rain in the next two hours, and a rain map with live radar
• A 10-day forecast on one shared scale; tap a day for its hours, rain and wind
• Feels like, humidity and dew point, wind and gusts, UV, visibility, precipitation, cloud cover and the moon
• Air quality, pollen where it's measured, and how today compares with the usual and the records
• How colourful the next sunrise and sunset are likely to be

SEVERE WEATHER (UNITED STATES)
• Warnings, watches and advisories from the US National Weather Service, most serious first
• Optional notifications for new alerts and for rain starting soon (off unless you turn them on)
• Alerts can be late or missing, so always follow official warnings. Two Degrees isn't affiliated with the National Weather Service or any government.

WIDGETS
• A Home screen widget you can resize: small, medium with the next hours, or large with six days
• It shows your Two Degrees city, or a city of its own
• Tap it to open that city in the app

MADE TO BE READ
• Follows your phone's font size, with five text sizes and a choice of two fonts
• TalkBack reads temperatures in both units
• Wind in mph, km/h, m/s or knots, and rain in inches or millimetres

PRIVATE BY DESIGN
No account, no ads, no tracking. Your cities stay on your phone: only their locations, and the places you search for, are sent to get the weather. If you use My Location, it's rounded to about a kilometre first.

Free and open source (MIT License). Made by Bradley Cowdrey. Weather data by Open-Meteo.com, alerts from the US National Weather Service, radar from RainViewer, maps from OpenFreeMap, places from GeoNames.
